tagline.text: A hidden 50 m cliff waterfall and a cluster of falls below Mount Romelo's ridge

location.label: Location
location.text: Mount Romelo, Brgy. Macatad, Siniloan, Laguna

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱900–1,700 (transport and food from Manila, per person)

children.text: Buruwisan Falls is a waterfall about 50 m high, tucked below the ridge of Mount Romelo in Siniloan, Laguna. A muddy forest trail from Barangay Macatad leads down to an emerald pool, with Lanzones and Batya-Batya Falls nearby.

Buruwisan Falls lies in Barangay Macatad in Siniloan, at the eastern end of Laguna province. It hangs on the upper Siniloan River, which rises on Mount Romelo (the southwestern tip of the Sierra Madre), and drops about

. English Wikipedia describes it as the most popular of the river's five best-known falls because it is the easiest to reach. It has long been the destination of Mount Romelo hikes. A 2008 travel blog noted that its emerald water and nearly vertical rock wall make it popular for rappelling and swimming, and Wikipedia calls it a training ground for novice climbers.
You do not visit the falls on their own; the trip is bundled with a Mount Romelo hike. You start at the registration point near the Macatad barangay hall, walk about
3km

of forest trail, pass the campsite on the ridge, and descend a steep slope to the top and bottom pools of the falls. You can make it a day trip from Manila with a very early start, but the one-night version with a camp on the ridge is more common. The route runs roughly registration point, first rest stop, ridge campsite, falls. Times differ by report, but the walk from registration to the falls usually takes 3–4 hours, and up to 5 hours in wet weather.

Around the main falls are Lanzones Falls, Batya-Batya (Guiling-Guiling) Falls, Sampaloc Falls and Sapang Labo Falls, and with enough water the trail extends to Binaytuan, Diwata, Twin and Sebakon Falls. Local guides say there are about a dozen falls in the area. You cannot see them all in a day, so for a day trip pick three or four. Height and difficulty differ from falls to falls. The main falls and Lanzones are relatively easy, Batya-Batya requires a chest-deep canyon crossing, Sapang Labo is the farthest, and Twin Falls can only be reached with ropes.

The mountain itself suits beginners, but the descent to the falls is muddy and steep and takes real effort. A guide is practically required, and rain makes the trail slippery enough to double your time. The village manages the site and collects the fees, so check prices and rules with the Macatad barangay hall before you go. The ridge campsite has long been criticized as overly commercialized. Weekends get crowded with local youth and group hikers, so go on a weekday if you want some quiet.

The falls drop about 50–55 m down a nearly vertical rock wall into a deep, cold emerald pool. They are known as a rappelling spot, and in the wet season the spray at the base is impressive. The main falls sit right below the campsite, so the view looking down from above is completely different from the view looking up from the pool.
A waterfall about 21–30 m high, a few minutes' walk upstream from the main falls. It is named after the lanzones trees that grow nearby. It is quieter than the main falls and makes a good photo spot.

Also called Guiling-Guiling Falls, this is a two-tier waterfall. The pool below the second tier is reported to be around 5 m deep and is good for swimming, but the way there includes a chest-deep canyon crossing, so a guide is a must.

A flat clearing near the ridge top can hold dozens of tents. It is a 10–15 minute walk above Buruwisan Falls, so you can head down early in the morning and have the falls to yourself. Reviews say there is no toilet or running water there, so come well prepared.

Part of Old Buruwisan Falls, above the main falls, can only be reached by rappelling, and Binaytuan Falls is described as the one with the biggest drop. These are remote and not part of the usual route, so talk to an experienced guide.
Sampaloc Falls is about 12 m high and lies farther upstream. Sapang Labo Falls is a two-tier waterfall with a waist-deep pool. Both are far away, so be ready for leeches and slippery trails.
The red volcanic clay of Mount Romelo gets as slick as chocolate when wet, and locals call it Romelo Chocolate. Climbing down using tree roots as a ladder is half the fun of the trek.

children.text: Take a van or bus toward Siniloan from Shaw Boulevard or Legarda in Manila. It takes about 3–4 hours, so leave early.

Rest near the campsite, then descend the steep slope to the Buruwisan Falls pool for a swim and photos.
Make a short side trip up to Lanzones Falls and have lunch.
Climb back up and walk down to the registration point, which takes about

. Wash up at the village toilets (
) and catch a ride home.
A day trip is tight, and it can get dark if it rains. A one-night trip is better if you want plenty of time in the water.
Register at the registration point, hire a guide, and carry your gear up to the ridge campsite. If your load is heavy, you can use a horse (about
one way) or a porter (about
one way).
Pitch your tent and cook dinner. Some reviews mention a spring, but it is safer to bring plenty of drinking water. Mobile signal is poor.
Wake up around sunrise, have breakfast and pack up the camp.
Descend the steep slope to swim at Buruwisan Falls, then visit Lanzones Falls and Batya-Batya Falls.
Have lunch and hike down. Carry all your trash back out.

The best time is the dry season, from November to April. The trails are less slippery and the stream is low, which makes the canyon crossings safer.

In February to April, however, some falls shrink or dry up, and reports differ. For falls with plenty of water, aim for November to January or the end of the rainy season, and ask the village about the state of the falls before you go.

Easiest walking, but some falls dry up. Bring plenty of water and a hat.
Afternoon showers increase and the trail turns muddy again.
Extreme mud and the stream floods. Access is closed during typhoon warnings.

There are few places to stay in Barangay Macatad and Siniloan town, so most people pitch a tent at the ridge campsite. Reviews mention a small shop and a few huts there, but it has become commercialized, so do not expect much. Bring your own tent, mat, cooking gear and trash bags.

Buy food at Siniloan market or at the eateries and shops near the registration point. Along the trail, you may find only snacks for sale. Open fires near the falls risk starting a forest fire, so use only a portable stove. For lodging, check options in Siniloan town.
For washing up, use the toilet and shower near the barangay hall for about

. After the hike you can rest at Siniloan town or at a restaurant such as Kia3 at the village entrance. Shop hours in the area are irregular, so buy snacks and water in Siniloan in advance. Check locally for anything else you need.
Register at the Greenhouse (near the barangay hall) and always climb with a local guide. Past stories of theft and accidents make solo day hikes unwise.
On a day trip, choose only three or four falls. The main falls and Lanzones Falls alone are very rewarding.
Bring hiking boots and an extra pair of socks, and gloves help with gripping tree roots. Some reviews mention that boot rental (about ₱100) is available locally.
Carry 1.5–2 L of drinking water and plenty of cash. It is not confirmed whether GCash is accepted.
Leeches are common in the wet season. Bring long pants, mosquito and leech repellent, and salt or alcohol.
Fixed ropes on the descent may be worn, so tug on them first and follow your guide's instructions.
Phone signal is weak, so save maps and contact numbers beforehand and tell your companions your plan.
Take all your trash back out, and never light fires carelessly.
Before leaving, ask the Macatad barangay hall (the contact number in reviews may change) about water levels, trail conditions and guide availability.
Do not go if it is raining or a typhoon is forecast, because mud and stream flooding make it very dangerous; check first with the village whether access is open.
Parts of the descent to the falls are steeper than 60 degrees, and you grip wet rock and tree roots on the way down. Injuries are frequent, so go slowly.
People have been injured on Tarzan-style vine jumps above the falls, so do not try them.
The canyon can rise suddenly in the wet season. If it rains upstream, move to high ground immediately.
Swim only where your guide says it is safe; the pool is deep and cold.
Prices and rules differ between reports and change, so check the latest notice at the Macatad barangay hall.
The best-known gorge waterfall in Laguna, famous for its bangka rapids ride. Travel time varies with traffic, so check locally.
A church in Mabitac, which you pass on the zigzag road on the way to Siniloan. It is a registered site and worth a stop along the way.
A town at the eastern end of Laguna de Bay that serves as the transit base. You can buy supplies at the market and find tricycles.
